en: Oṃ! Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Having prostrated before the Bodhisattvas and the Noble Saṅgha,
this commentary on the *Jātakamālā*, entitled *Yaśaskaraguṇodayā*, is composed.

In this regard, the venerable master Śūra, the son of a southern king, having renounced his kingdom even though it had come to him by succession, went forth into homelessness and set out upon the path to enlightenment. Abiding on the first stage (*bhūmi*), in order to easily lead the world onto the path to enlightenment through the gateway of compassion and the discourse of the Sugata, he composed the *Jātakamālā* while walking during a period of emergence from meditative absorption, writing the characters with thorns upon *tamāla* leaves.

This work is called the *Jātakamālā* because it consists of narratives (*kathā*). For it likewise instructs in the four aims of human life, with the dharma of liberation as its primary focus; it is extensive due to its description of the undertaking of many births through a mixture of prose and verse; it has a single locus because it is the sole cause for the continuum of the omniscient one's knowledge; and it culminates in exaltation because it is established through such a sequence belonging to Śākyamuni alone.

However, the chapters (*parvan*) therein consist of mutually distinct subject matters, like those in the *Bhārata* narrative; and while worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) was proclaimed there for figures such as the *cāraṇas* and Yudhiṣṭhira, here it is the prosperity pertaining to supramundane knowledge (*lokottarajñāna*) that is intended, which does not depend upon the physical body. This is just as in that same work, in the "Ascent to Heaven" (*svargārohaṇa*), concerning Yudhiṣṭhira and the others. Thus has the name "Campū" been explained.

According to Śrī Daṇḍin, it is said: "That which consists of both prose and verse and has meaning as its form is called *campū*. Alternatively, this is a composition in the *jāti* style, because it is a narrative following exactly the manner in which the Dharma known as the *Jātakas* was taught by the Tathāgata. Furthermore, the sequence intended here is based solely on the *pāramitās*, not on the order of births. For while the Blessed One previously gave massages and so forth while fulfilling the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*), he did not do so according to this specific chronological sequence.

In this way, it should be understood that the same applies to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) and the others; and by stating "it should be spoken thus," etc., the illustrative example was given in order to instruct those who teach the Dharma for the sake of benefiting the world. Therein, first, in order to show the connection as a factor for engagement and the subject matter (*abhidheya*), he speaks a hymn of praise preceded by worship for the marvelous deeds (*caritādbhuta*) which constitute the nature of the subject matter.

"Those who possess glory," and so forth. The act of salutation will be made explicit at the beginning of the narrative, though it was already indicated in the introduction by the statement, "I shall worship. The word *śrī* is employed at the outset; *śrī* is the perfection of one's own and others' welfare. Those in whom this exists are [the ones referred to].

Because they are endowed with the perfection of self-interest and the perfection of the welfare of others, he will state that these are "glorious" (*śrīmanti*), being marvelous deeds from former births. The virtues of good persons (*satpuruṣāṇām guṇāḥ*)— or, alternatively,
their "good virtues" (*sadguṇāḥ*) meaning excellent virtues— such as compassion, patience, truthfulness, magnanimity, heroism, and so forth, are cultivated (*guṇyante*).

Because those who seek prosperity (*śrī*) bestow it [upon others], their acceptance—that is, their appropriation—is auspicious (*maṅgala*). Those [names] in which there is the accomplishment of desired aims (*abhimatārthasiddhi*) through that [acceptance] are thus described. Alternatively, because they are causes of auspiciousness, they are auspicious; like the word *dākṣyādi*, they are auspicious as "praiseworthy" (*praśasta*), and their recitation is [the subject].

Fame (*kīrti*) is renown; its bases (*āspada*) are the locations [of that fame]. Because they are sung by all people for the sake of merit and because they are marvelous, they are "unblemished" (*anavagīta*). Those [actions] which are censured by the perfected ones (*siddha*)—namely, those caused by the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth—are the opposite of those; therefore, they are "blameless" (*anindita*). And these are the joy of the worlds...

They are called "mind-captivating" (*manohara*) because they carry away the minds. For even [teachings] such as the meditation on the foul (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), though not ill-spoken, do not become mind-captivating for everyone. First—

However, the marvelous deeds of Janma are faultless and beyond reproach, as they have not been censured by anyone.

And [these qualities] are captivating to the minds of all people. Because the Sage has understood all categories of objects exactly as they are through reflection in every respect—or because of his engagement in the silence of body, speech, and mind—the Blessed One is omniscient. [This refers to] those [qualities] which preceded the state of Buddhahood spoken of by the Sugata.
Among those births, there are deeds that have been performed which are of a marvelous nature and of a wondrous nature;

or rather, among the deeds, those which are of a marvelous nature—those very deeds I shall worship. This is the connection, using the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the sense of the agent's intention (*kartṛ-abhiprāya*).
The suffix -ta is used in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*). By the word "devotion" (*bhaktyā*), the bowing of body and mind is indicated;

the bowing of speech, however, is expressed by the words "his own poem," and so forth. This "own poem" refers to that which is intended to be composed by the teacher Śūra in the form of a narrative called the *Jātakamālā*—that is, a "handful of flowers."

"Like a bouquet of flowers" (*kusumāñjali*) means a collection of flowers; because it is variegated, fragrant, and charming. By this phrase, he has declared the connection and the subject matter (*abhidheya*), namely that this poem is an "offering" (*arcana*) to those whose deeds are marvelous, since it serves to illustrate them.
Now, since the poet is not an eyewitness, how were the deeds of the Sage in his previous births known?

To this it is replied: because the Sage himself recounted them in the form of illustrative narratives (*nidarśana*) within various *sūtras* and *anta*s, in the course of teaching the Dharma for the purpose of winning over the assembly. As he will state [later]: "That which is heard from the *ṛṣis*..."

Regarding the passage beginning with "by means of reasoning" (*yuktyā*): if this is so, those [reasonings] already exist; what is the use of this poem, since it contains no unprecedented subject matter?

This is true; however, the investigation of many *sūtra* passages is difficult for those of little effort, and they do not engage in it. But in this poem, those [passages] are found together in one place without exertion.

They are seen; and a different aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) arises from poetry. Furthermore, just as the Tathāgata himself recounted his own deeds for the sake of the welfare of the world, so too shall I, through my own poem, relate those [deeds] found even in the words of others, having gathered them together.

He states the purpose with the two verses beginning with "ślāghyaiḥ" (v. 1.4). Therein, by the phrase "for the sake of the world," the purpose for undertaking [this work] as an invisible cause (*adṛṣṭa-hetu*) is stated; and by the phrase "the state of being dear to the learned for the sake of making what is unintelligible intelligible," the visible cause (*dṛṣṭa*) is also stated. Thus, these are the visible and invisible purposes.

It is stated that the *Jātakamālā* was composed for the sake of [the benefit] of people; furthermore, for the listeners as well, it serves to provide a single-pointed vision of the deeds of the Bodhisattvas, a thorough understanding of the path to Sugata-hood, and the clarification of the mind.

The purpose [of this work] is as follows: therein, they are "praiseworthy" (*ślāghya*) because they deserve praise due to being endowed with all virtues; "by these" means by these wonders (*adbhuta*) being described by me through my own poem; and those "by which the path of the Sugata is marked" (*cihnita*) means those by which the path of the Sugata is known.

Likewise; the meaning is "by the true signs of the path to awakening. Here, the word *bhūta* denotes existence, as in the expression *bodhisattvabhūta*, which means "being a bodhisattva. And those signs are both manifest and subtle; such is the case.

Since well-known [reasons] are seen to be non-deviant, while those that are not well-known are seen to be doubtful, he says: "by means of well-known or clearly characterized manifestations. This means by means of those that are non-deviant. (11) It is "taught" (*deśita*) or "manifested" (*prakāśita*) on all sides (*ā*). The word *yat* means "because" (*yasmāt*).

The term *sugata* is a *nipāta* (an indeclinable particle used as a name). Because he has abandoned the obscurations of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obscurations to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), he speaks with what is truly excellent and beautiful;
thus, he is "Well-Gone" (*sugata*) because he is unlike any other. His true nature (*sadbhāva*) consists of unsurpassed gnosis (*anuttarajñāna*) and the possession of all capacities.
That by which this [nature] is sought is the Path (*mārga*). And that [Path] consists of the perfections (*pāramitā*) such as generosity (*dāna*), and so forth.

It is cultivated as having the characteristic of nobility due to its profundity. In that regard, the awakening to the self-nature of all phenomena in their vastness is what will be stated: "The Blessed One has become the self of all beings.
By means of this, being embraced by great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), one proceeds toward generosity and the other perfections, free from faults such as envy and stinginess.

Through the power of mental attention based on resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manaskāra*), he attains nirvāṇa by relinquishing everything for all sentient beings. Profundity, however, is the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena; because of his awakening to the world, he dwells in equanimity, liberated from all attachments, proceeding through the complete purity of wisdom (*prajñā*).

By virtue of mental engagement with reality (*tattvamanaskāra*), one does not enter into cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). This very path, consisting of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*) and proceeding as a unified pair (*yuganaddha*), is called the direct path; and by way of succession, it is the Noble Eightfold Path.
Namely: right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), right speech (*samyagvāk*), right... [1] ...right... [1] ...right.
The final member consists of right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

Thus, the twofold path has been pointed out and explained; the meaning is that just as a path is described to someone unfamiliar with the way by means of well-marked trees, groves, and so forth, so too is it described by these [qualities]. It is harsh, ungentle toward sentient beings, and characterized by a nature such as violence and the like.

He states "those whose minds [are merciless]" and so forth for the sake of following the conduct of the virtuous, even toward one who is devoid of compassion and associated with cruelty. Furthermore, the pacification of obstacles occurs here through the beginning and end of the *Bodhisattvacarita*.
He is indeed perfected through the act of glorification (*kīrtana*). If this is so, what is the purpose of a separate salutation and praise?

For that which is a verbal salutation exists here continuously as part of the [recitation of] deeds, since it is for the sake of praise. True; the former deeds are glorified here, not the perfected one.

...the state. For this very reason, the Blessed One, established in the form of the Three Jewels, is honored. The word *artha* signifies purpose (*prayojana*). In that regard, he moves and proceeds; thus, by the rule *careṣ ṭa*, the suffix *ta* is applied. The qualities (*guṇa*) are those such as the "approaching" ones (*ābhigāmika*), and their practice (*pratipatti*)—

"Accomplishment" (anusthānam) means "fulfillment" (sampādanam). Alternatively, by virtue of the reverence for practice or the reverence born of [his] qualities, there is "splendor," meaning "brilliance" or "radiance.
"Was followed" (anvagamyata) means "was reached"; the sense is that it was not even subsequently attained.

The form *anvagamyata* is derived from the root *gam* with the prefix *anu-* and the suffix *laṇ* (the passive marker) in the sense of an object. One who knows all reality—both what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted—in every aspect and through all indicative signs is "omniscient" (*sarvajña*).
The word *iti* here indicates a reversal of the meaning of the term; by means of it, the word "omniscient" is withdrawn from its literal referent.

It is established in its own nature, as in the expression "this person said, 'cow'. In that context, those syllables which are phonemes (*varṇa*) are non-false (*avitatha*), meaning they possess a true referent (*satyārtha*). This is because the object to be expressed exists in that very manner.
Because they possess the nature of the *Jātakamālāṭīkā*, they do not convey [mere] designations (*saṃjñā*). By means of those unerring syllables,
there is a radiant and blazing fame— namely, the proclamation or the renown that he is "the Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*).

Because it is well-known in the world that "the Blessed One is omniscient," the collection of phonemes belonging to him is meaningful; however, according to the position that it is not the individual phonemes [that are meaningful], it is the sentence (*vākya*) or the sphoṭa that is called the "imperishable" (*akṣara*), because it does not decay. In that context, the term "omniscient" refers to that which is non-false and possesses a true object.

That which will be stated [hereafter], by that it is "blazing"; this is pride (*māna*). Alternatively, as for this fame that "he is omniscient" (*sarvajña*), its meaning is that the syllables follow an unfailing truth and are imperishable (*akṣaya*).
The summary and so forth are as before. By the word "on the crown," through this prostration of the body, the mind—

Since bodily activity is preceded by the mind, "I bow" (*name*) refers to that as well; furthermore, by this [phrase] "I bow," vocal prostration is also included. Thus, it should be understood that the threefold prostration has been performed.
In the expression "I bow" (*name*), because one bows while being bowed to for the sake of the Tathāgata’s qualities, the *ātmanepada* ending is used in the sense of the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*).

In the phrase *dam na duhasnunamam yakciṇau*, there is a prohibition of the *yak* suffix. Consequently, in the word *buddham*, the accusative case is used due to the distinction of it being the object (*karman*). Alternatively, because we observe such usage, the root *nam* is understood as being conjugated in both voices (*ubhayapadī*). Furthermore, this is a usage referring to the present tense, as it pertains to the act of paying homage (*namaskāra*).

Otherwise, for the sake of cutting off [doubt], one should say "having prostrated" and so forth. By the word "that" (*tam*), he refers back to what was stated by "of which" (*yasya*). "Unequaled" (*asama*) is because it is superior to the entire world.
"Dharma" is the twelvefold teaching; namely: the *sūtra*, the *geya*, the *vyākaraṇa*, and so on.
[The ninefold teaching consists of: *gāthā*, *udāna*, *nidāna*, *avadāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, and *upadeśa*.

The Saṃgha is the noble assembly of irreversible bodhisattvas and the eight types of great persons (*mahāpuruṣapudgala*); together with these two, it forms a compound in the sense of equal connection (*tulyayoga*), yet even in such a compound, the form *saha* does not undergo the change to *sa*.
Or rather, it occurs because [the rule] "or of a subordinate element" (upasarjanasya) is optional.

Now, by means of the introductory discourse, he introduces the general meaning (*samudāyārtha*) with the prose passage beginning with "In all sentient beings" (*sarvasattveṣu*). It should be understood that the introduction of the general meaning occurs through this introductory prose which sets forth what is to be established (*pratijñāta*). In that very context, because it is the foremost of the perfections (*pāramitā*), it is generosity (*dāna*).
First, it is stated that [generosity] is of four kinds, distinguished by the giving of material things (*āmiṣa*), the Dharma, fearlessness, and assistance.
The giving of material things is also fourfold, distinguished by the giving of wealth, what is beyond wealth, limbs, and ointments.
"Wealth" refers to money, grain, and so forth; "what is beyond wealth" refers to children, wives, and so forth; "limbs" refers to hands...

[This refers to] the feet and so forth; the ointment for the head, bones, eyes, body, and so forth. In this *Jātaka*, there is only the gift of the body. And showing that this is accomplished by one who possesses great compassion arising from great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), and not by anyone else, he says: "toward all sentient beings," and so forth.

"Every sentient being" refers to gods, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, hell-beings, and so forth. "Without cause" means that it is out of compassion alone, without regard for any fruit such as a reciprocal benefit; whereas for all others, even for animals, there is always a connection to a cause. This is the supreme [compassion].

It is supramundane because it is free from defilement; it is affectionate and loving because it removes all suffering. Its nature is such that its form is uncreated. By this, great compassion is expressed.
All beings—whether stable or moving—are one's own self, not other than oneself.

"Those who have broken [the barriers]" refers to one for whom self and others are equal; by this, great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) is described as having existed even in previous births, and not merely in the state of the final existence. "Bhagavān" is a term of veneration. He is a Buddha because of his awakening to the reality of things exactly as they are.
Since the object of the understanding of the meaning [of the Buddha] is not intended as a grammatical object (*karma*), the suffix *-ta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
Thus, "toward him [the Buddha], there should be clarity" means that devotion (*bhakti*) should be practiced with a mind free from defilement. For example—
The two words *jātakamālātīkā* and *śabda* are used for the purpose of illustration. Here, the word *śruti* refers to an uninterrupted tradition (*avichinnā*), as it is said:
"What is heard here? It is an *avadāna*. An *avadāna* is that which is pure (*śuddha*).
The meaning is that it is the performed action (*karmacarita*). That which is stated as an illustration for the sake of another's understanding is called "news" (*vārttā*).
And in order to state that this news possesses the status of scripture (*āgama*), he says: "The Three Jewels," and so forth.
Because they are the most excellent of all things, the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha are "jewels. That very same Three Jewels are the Guru.
"Those for whom [the Guru] is most worthy of being served because they have no other refuge"—this is how our own Gurus will say it.

This is an epithet of him, and the following two points are also to be stated: "Practice" (*pratipatti*) is the performance of what has been taught by the Guru; that itself is a "quality" (*guṇa*) because it is of the nature of the dharma that removes the afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). By that very [quality]...

Those by whom the Gurus—the Triple Gem and so forth—have been propitiated through their virtues and direct devotion are "those [who have thus propitiated the Gurus]. Through the accumulation—that is, the mass—of virtues such as faith, ethical discipline, and learning, those Gurus are "great"; by them, our own Gurus, the poet [addresses] his most venerable teachers with humility.

By means of the teaching that sets forth the Dharma, he refers to the preceptors and others; the sense is that because such persons speak without falsehood, this discourse has truth as its object. "Bodhi" is a designation for the suchness of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-tathatā*). In that regard, one who possesses the being (*sattva*)—that is, the mind—is a *bodhisattva*. <1> Ya-...

They are called *bodhisattvas* because they have made a vow for enlightenment; they are called *mahāsattvas* because they bring about the perfect accomplishment of the welfare of all sentient beings. He will state the verb "took" (*cakāra*) regarding the assumption of birth; by using the particle "it is said" (*kila*), he indicates that these matters are not within his direct perception. This must necessarily be done by me...
A thesis (*pratijñā*) is the acceptance of a specific object determined as "this must be done.

Its excellence (*atiśaya*) consists in this: that one should always, in every place, having removed all sentient beings from all sufferings, establish them in unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*) by providing them with every means of happiness.

"Should be honored" means that one makes a formal commitment through speech, as if in the presence of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and their practices. "In a manner that is similar and appropriate" refers to this specific action by which one favors [others] accordingly. This is done by means of the four bases of sympathy (*saṃgrahavastu*).

Regarding the benefit of the world (*lokānugraha*) spoken by the Blessed One, he says "giving" (*dāna*) and so forth. Beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*) is its application—

The term "beginning with" (*prabhṛti*) expresses the same meaning as "acting for the sake of others" (*janakāritva*). Furthermore, "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*) refers to the introduction of those to be trained (*vineya*) into that very same path of merit in which one has oneself established;
it means acting with a single purpose for the sake of their conviction. From the use of the plural, [it follows] the pursuit of [others' welfare] and the teaching of what is beneficial.

The [perfections] beginning with generosity are included. Wisdom, characterized by the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), is the thorough knowledge of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things.

The inclusion of that [wisdom] is the purification of generosity and the other perfections by means of it; therefore, they become faultless and pure. Without wisdom, however, their fruits are meager and subject to exhaustion.

Thus, they are not faultless. In that regard, the purity of giving consists in the application of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) and the absence of expectation for karmic maturation (*vipāka*). The purity of kind speech and the other [means of attraction] consists in the absence of desire for gain and the lack of regard for reciprocal benefit. For he says that "benefit" (*artha*) is the favoring of the world; [this is] compassion (*kāruṇya*).

Regarding the term "outflows" (*niṣyanda*): compassion (*karuṇā*) is characterized by the protection of beings from suffering. Its state is compassionateness (*kāruṇya*), which means a mind accompanied by sorrow. That which is similar to this is its outflow; the meaning is that this practice of giving and so forth has the nature of a continuous stream of pity. Thus, through wisdom and compassion—

This benefit to the three worlds through giving and so forth is the cause of Buddhahood; therefore, it is not purposeless. For Bodhisattvas do not benefit others through giving and so forth out of a desire for a [personal] fruit;
rather, this is simply the natural outflow of compassion, in that, unable to endure the suffering of others, they [sacrifice] their own bodies.

Moreover, they renounce [worldly things]. And "favor" consists in winning over [beings] through giving and so forth, and establishing them in unexcelled perfect enlightenment. The specific duty (*svadharma*) of Brahmins consists of the six activities: sacrificing for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, studying, teaching, giving, and receiving gifts; therein lies non-attachment.
By her, [the performance] was presented; "vṛtti" means conduct or livelihood (*vartana*).

Medinikara states: "Vṛtti refers to the exposition, the means of subsistence, and the employment of the *kaiśikī*, *ārabhaṭī*, and other styles. Thus, it refers to the *vṛtti* such as *kaiśikī*, *ārabhaṭī*, and so forth.

The specific commentary on Vāgbhaṭa’s *Ālaṃkāra* [states]: "That which exists for the maintenance of men is thus. [In the word *uditodite*,] the augment *num* is applied by the rule *iko 'ci vibhaktau*. By this, the perfection of conduct and the perfection of wealth are declared;
he speaks of the perfection of renown due to noble birth with the words "uditodita" (*udita-udita*). "Uditam" [means...]
"Exalted" means excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.

It is "great" because it is honored by the world, or because it is vast due to having a wide circle of kinsmen. By the word "appropriation," the Bodhisattva's independence regarding his own birth is indicated; [it occurs] through the power of his vow.
By virtue of his mastery, he has arisen of his own accord and is not impelled by karma, unlike others who possess [only] equanimity.
For the birth of living beings arises from karma and afflictions (*kleśa*), and affliction consists of passion (*rāga*) and so forth;
however, for the Bodhisattva, all unwholesome karma and afflictions have been completely eliminated through the purification of wisdom.

The characteristic activity of the perfections is as follows: through compassion, there is established a form of attachment consisting of affection for afflicted sentient beings, by virtue of which he takes up birth for the sake of favoring those to be trained. "He" refers to the bodhisattva. He will explain the activity of the teacher, which consists of the act of sowing [the seeds].

The sequence and order of the *saṃskāras* belongs to him; he is thus [described]. What are those *saṃskāras*? He says: "by means of the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and so forth. That *saṃskāra* which is prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* at birth is the birth-rite. By the word "and so forth," [are meant] the naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first sight of the sun (*sūryadarśana*), and so on.

In this context, only the sequence of the *prāśana*, *cūḍākarma*, and *upanayana* is intended to be included, because the remaining sacraments (*saṃskāra*) are yet to be performed. "Emaciated," and so forth. *Kṣud* means hunger; by that hunger (*kṣudhā*), the suffix *niṣṭhā* [is applied to the root] *cho*, meaning "to cut. "Would be experienced" means it would be perceived. The phrase "wandering about" refers to the scattering of flowers due to their falling from afar with the force of the wind. The singular number is used because the genus (*jāti*) is intended. By the expression "colored by sandalwood powder," [the author indicates] the sandalwood...
Nor was even the scattering of powder mentioned. They arrived; by implication, they had already come, having seen [the sight].

The word *apsarogaṇaiḥ* (by hosts of apsarases, i.e., celestial nymphs) is formed with the compound *sa-* [from *saha*], yet the substitution of *sa-* for *saha-* was not applied, as in the rule *vopasarjanasya*. *Vavau* means "he blew" (*vāti sma*). *Manojñā* means "pleasing to the mind."

"Whose [qualities] are coolness, softness, fragrance, and so forth, belonging to the wind (*samīraṇa*)—he is thus described. Regarding the word "of the worlds" (*jagatām*), by the rule of *ekaśeṣa* for identical forms, there is the inclusion of all three worlds.
"The joy of the mind" (*manaḥpraharṣaḥ*) means the delight of the heart; "expanded" (*jṛmbhitaḥ*) means fully blossomed or arisen.

The meaning is as follows: those hosts of beings (*bhūtagaṇa*), that is, multitudes of living creatures, whose minds were thus pervaded and filled with joy; likewise, by those possessed of great supernatural power (*maharddhi*)—that is, great majesty (*vibhūti*)—who were struck with wonder (*savismaya*), words (*giraḥ*) were uttered (*udīritāḥ*), that is, spoken aloud.

The connection is that "auspicious" (*śubhāḥ*) means "praiseworthy" (*praśastāḥ*) and "were heard" (*śuśruvire*) means "were listened to" (*śrutāḥ*). Furthermore, the king’s extraordinary deed was the gift of his eyes and the production of that [gift] through the power of his truthful resolve (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).
His "praise" (*stavaḥ*) is a hymn (*stotra*); those [verses] are its basis and are connected to it. And those words are the basis for the hymn.
He speaks with these two verses beginning with "Aho.
"Aho" expresses wonder; "bata" expresses joy. Magnanimity (*audārya*) is the state of being unconfined (*asaṃkaṭatā*). Purity (*viśuddhi*)...
It is established because of the departure from the stain of stinginess.

Behold how, in what manner, there is this purity of the mind of this king; behold his magnanimity and compassion, which are of a wondrous nature. The meaning is that they have become manifest. Behold this purity!
The alternative reading *vāsya cetasaḥ* is indeed clear. "Free from longing" (*nirutsukā*) means devoid of yearning.

He states that one who is of such a nature becomes worthy of homage even by gods and others, beginning with the words "Homage be to... and so forth. His fortitude and prowess are truly marvelous (*adbhuta*), being of a wondrous nature.
He who is thus addressed: "When you were blind, the world was without a protector; now it has once again attained a protector. His lotus-eye, like a lotus, has regained its sight;
by him—by you, 'sat' (the good one)—whose splendor and beauty have blossomed and opened."

The meaning is as follows: the accumulations—that is, the heaps—of merits consisting of giving, morality, and meditative cultivation have not been in vain; that is, they were not fruitless. For this reason, he has once again attained an even more distinguished eye. Therefore, it is said: "By means of the Dharma, victory has been won," meaning the defeat of adversaries has been achieved. "After a long time" means...

The particle *kathaṃcit*, which resembles a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), has the sense of "for a long time"; [it means] "forcibly" (*prasahyam*) [conquered]. For it was conquered by means of the Dharma, as evidenced by the manifestation of the empowerment of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth before all people. The word *khalu* is used as an ornament for the sentence. Thus [is the victory] of the hosts of *bhūtas*.
"Of the words of praise heard from all sides"—thus there is not a single sentence [here].

"Having propitiated and satisfied this king"—[this refers to him]. "O you whose intention (*āśaya*) is pure"—this is an address; "intention" means purpose, and it is not that it is unknown to us, but rather it is indeed known.

Thus, because you are dear to the petitioner, there is no water [to be given] that does not exist for you. In this way, since you have been made to perform a true resolve (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*) out of your zeal, by that means those two eyes of yours were restored and returned to me. By this, it is said as follows: by me—

Or rather, [it was] by the guise of a *vaṇḍha* brahmin that your eyes were seized, and not by anyone else; thus there is the restoration of those two. Their minds were filled—that is, pervaded—by wonder and joy from seeing the Lord’s divine vision; likewise, even the dull [were made] more dull.
The meaning is "extremely slow. With such glances in their eyes—
eyes that were wide open and dilated out of a desire for uninterrupted sight— and followed by ministers, kinsmen, and citizens who had attached themselves from behind, he [proceeded].

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: having departed from that garden and approached while gazing upon that excellent city, he went and taught the Dharma. "Being spread out" means being expanded by prosperity brought about by the rising of the king's fame; and "beauty" refers to the cleansing of hair, the various kinds of flowers, and so forth.

That which is thus [described] is its receptacle and its accumulation. "In this way" refers to what is about to be stated. That in which the self (*ātman*) is brought forward—that is, exemplified—is called *ātmopanāmyika*;
the meaning is "the demonstration of the self. (11) He says that: "Who indeed," and so forth.
Divine (*divya*) means belonging to heaven (*divi-bhava*). Their power (*prabhāva*) is such that they can be seen from a hundred *yojanas* away.
"By the merit (*puṇya*) resulting from the gift"—that is, when [the recipient] has approached and arrived; therefore, [it is said] "and the gift."

"Even from a hundred" means either from less than a hundred (*śatād avarena*) or, by the elision of the *lyap* suffix, the ablative case indicates reaching even a hundred (*śatam apy āsādya*). "Visible" (*dṛśyam*) means fit for seeing, that which is graspable by the eye.

This is the meaning. "As if situated not far away" (*adūrasthitam iva*) means "clearly manifest as if not far away" (*adūrasthitavispaṣṭam*), which is to say, "distinctly. "In all directions" (*sarvataḥ*) means in all ten directions.
Compassion toward other beings; or, compassion that is supreme or excellent. Discipline.

Virtue (*śīla*). From those two, "well-born" means produced. This is the meaning: what is the gift of one possessing virtue through compassion? [1] What indeed could be another or superior means for the sake of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*)? The meaning is that there is none at all. [It is] giving.
"How is it certain that this alone is the means for higher rebirth (*abhyudaya*)? To this he says: "Because," and so forth.
For [the Buddha] cites himself as an example with the words beginning "the human eye" and so on;
for in this very life, this mere flower has been obtained, whereas the fruit is the unsurpassed realization (*anuttarādhigama*).
It will be so. [They] have attained that divine eye (*divyam cakṣuḥ*) which belongs to non-human beings such as gods and others.

Alternatively, because it is similar to a human eye in terms of blinking and so forth, it is "human," yet because of its connection with divine power, it is also "divine. This is explained [in the commentary] without [the word] *tatra*. "The Śibis" is a designation for a region.
This is the address. (5) Regarding "in the other world," that is, in the next life:

through giving, one is reborn possessing enjoyments, and from enjoyment comes happiness; therefore, giving alone is the path for the arising of happiness in the next world—the way that serves as the means of attainment. And in this world, [it protects against] the fear of kings, thieves, fire, water, and so forth—

Free from people and being honored by them, he sleeps happily and wakes up happily. Furthermore, fame arises from giving; therefore, that happiness is preeminent in fame. However, the happiness derived from wealth acquired through theft, gambling, and the like is not preeminent in fame. [Regarding] the enjoyment of giving—

The fruit is wealth; this very point is expressed by the passage beginning with "of wealth," etc. It is "pithless" because it does not endure for long, and "light" because it is subject to calamities. It is "substantial" (*sāra*); for elsewhere it is said: "Substance (*sāra*) refers to strength, marrow, the firm part, justice, water, and wealth."

[The full explanation follows: Through generosity, its long-term endurance is secured. "Worlds" refers to one's own and other sentient beings; "benefit for them" means being oriented toward and inclined toward that [benefit]. Therefore, even the renunciation of one’s own enjoyments is indeed generosity because of the excellence of the underlying intention (*āśaya*). A "treasure" (*nidhāna*) is a hoard (*nidhi*) that lasts for a long time.
Because it persists. "Nidhana" means destruction (*vināśa*). That which has a single finality (*ekā niṣṭhā*) as its conclusion (*avasāna*) is so described;
the meaning is that it exists until the state of destruction.
Having thus concluded the Jātaka with the words "In this way," he connects it to the matter previously introduced:
the connection is that "in this manner, the greatness of the Tathāgata is to be proclaimed.
For indeed, the Blessed Tathāgatas are such great beings because, through the embrace of great compassion, [they were] previously...
In various births, they have shown compassion toward sentient beings by giving the gift of oil-massages;

and as was previously stated in the *Vyāghrījātaka*, "and so on as before," this Jātaka should likewise be recited here for the purpose of praising compassion, showing that compassion is the cause of benefiting others. Right here—

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "In this very life, the fruit of merits that have been performed and accumulated is seen"; and regarding the demonstration of that [fruit], it must be stated [as follows]. This very statement has been analyzed by [the author] himself with the words beginning with "thus" (*evam*). "Having honored" (*satkṛtya*) means the honoring of merits according to their [nature].

The accomplishment [of the vow]. By this, the purity of both the fundamental and the preparatory minds is stated. By the phrase "accumulated" (*upacitāni*) and "augmented" (*bahitāni*), the purity of the subsequent mind is also indicated. Thus, merits purified throughout the three times lead, in this very life, to the power of oneself—that is, to one's own capability.

They manifest merely as flowers in the form of excellence regarding enjoyments, physical bodies, and so forth, because the primary fruit arises in a future life; yet they are called "fruit" because they serve as the cause for that fruit. And that [fruit] is delightful through an uninterrupted continuity of fame.

The meaning is that it would be made beautiful by fame; yet such a thing is not possible. For how could Śakra, who possesses great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), even with a mere desire to test him, cause such injury to the eye of the Bodhisattva for even a single moment? Since, in this manner, the Bodhisattva—

The perfection of the gift of limbs was accomplished by Śakra solely for the sake of the Bodhisattva, and the world was incited toward merit because it witnessed the fruit of giving. For Śakra has, from the very beginning, possessed the thought of enlightenment and is ever intent on providing assistance to those who have set out for awakening; therefore—

Thus, because of the absence of defects in his intention, no evil arises for Śakra— whether born from the deficiency of a bodhisattva’s limbs or produced by deception; and because of its connection with King Śibi, it is called the "Śibi-jātaka."
In the Jātakamālāṭīkā, the second [tale], the Śibijātaka, is concluded.

Having thus explained great giving by means of two *jātaka*s, he now relates the *Kulmāṣapiṇḍī-jātaka* to show that even a small gift can set the world in motion. [Regarding] the ball of boiled beans (*kulmāṣapiṇḍī*):

What else could be small? In this regard, someone might think, "What will happen even by giving a small amount? To refute that, [the author], introducing the meaning of the whole, says "arisen from clarity of mind," and so forth. Clarity of mind (*cittaprasāda*) is a state of mind that is non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*).

The state of having a mind pervaded by faith (*śraddhā*), which consists of conviction and serene clarity; by this, the engagement in acts of returning favors and so forth, as well as the cessation of immoral conduct (*dauḥśīlya*), is described. "Vessel" (*pātra*), however, means a receptacle or support for qualities such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*); its excellence [is as follows].
It means that he is the substratum of variegated virtues, that is to say, free from all defects.

*Alpakam* means very little; the suffix *-ka* is used here either in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*) or in the sense of "a small amount" (*alpārthe*), thus meaning "extremely little. The word *nāma* is used in the sense of concession (*abhyupagame*). As for what you think—that there exists even a slight gift—that is not so.

That which is given is called a "gift" (*dāna*); here, it refers to the material object. And that, even if small in itself, is not small, because when accompanied by clarity of mind (*cittaprasāda*), it becomes of great fruit. Thus he says: "Because of the greatness of its maturation" (*vipāka-mahattvāt*). Maturation (*vipāka*) is the fruit of maturation; its greatness consists in [the attainment of] enjoyments (*bhoga*).

Because of the greatness of his virtues, such as his lack of pride, and because he remembers his past lives, the sense is that even a small gift should be given when accompanied by clarity of mind and so forth. In order to explain this very point in detail through a narrative, he says: "Tadyathā" (for example), etc. [The city] named Kośalā...

The constituent elements of the state (*janapada*), enthusiasm (*utsāha*), exertion (*udyoga*), counsel (*mantra*), the determination of what must be done (*kāryaviniścaya*), majesty (*prabhāva*), and prowess (*pratāpa*)—these are the powers (*śakti*) and capabilities (*samarthya*). Their attainment (*sampatti*) is their accumulation (*upacaya*). The word "beginning with" (*prabhṛti*) indicates a category; [it refers to] those things of this kind.

The word "of the [other] kings" (*ṣiṇām*) indicates excellence because of their lack of connection with faults. The meaning is that she made the splendor—that is, the abundance—of the qualities of a king, such as those leading to accessibility (*ābhigāmikatva*), surpassing, that is, rendered it preeminent. If one asks what this is, he says: "the beauty of the qualities of divine perfection. Divine perfection...

"His virtues," and so forth. Although these virtues belong to other kings as well, nevertheless, being adorned by his excellence of accumulated auspicious karma (*śubhakarma-sampad*), they shone even more brilliantly. Just as those whose beauty (*śrī*) or splendor has been unfolded and made to blossom by the autumn—the season of fall—[so did his virtues shine].

The meaning is that they shone like the rays of the moon. Fortune (*śrī*), or *lakṣmī*, abandoned—that is, left behind—the enemies and adversaries of that king, even though they were arrogant. This was because she followed his anger toward those who had taken refuge with him; [she abandoned] those who had become his friends and kinsmen among the king's dependents.
She took delight, she sported—*reme ramate sma*—as if she were *śrī-raktā*, like one who is full of passion; in this manner, by this way.
Regarding "among other lords of men" (*anyanarādhipeṣu*): those kings other than [the current] king, whether they are hostile to the king or dependent upon him;
[she was] one who followed his anger and favor within their domain, that is, in relation to that king.

Fortune (*śrī*) has come into being. She abandons those who are angry with the king; she serves like one who is devoted those whose minds are well-disposed toward the king. Thus, her conformity to anger and favor has been described. Thus, making that very point clear:
He said: "Because they have the nature of *dharma*, etc. For others are enemies;

their affliction is the torment [of them] by means of injury, killing, imprisonment, and so forth. If his intention toward that [affliction] is inauspicious—that is, not beneficial—the meaning is that it is certainly not [the case]. The word "nāma" indicates a slight diminution. Let this be so for now, as for what he...

Being of a righteous nature and having the dharma as his very essence, he certainly does not possess an unwholesome intention (*akalyāṇāśaya*). If so, how is it that he abandoned the royal parasol of Fortune? To this he says: "But [there was] devotion to his servants," and so forth. "Devotion" (*anurāga*) refers to the zeal or attachment toward the servants, that is, those who have taken refuge in him. Thus.
Thus, such an incomparable yawning manifested and arose,
by which Fortune, disregarding the master’s unique virtue and his affection for those who have taken refuge in him, [departed].

Having abandoned that very parasol along with its retinue, they have taken refuge in that [Jātakamālā] alone. Therefore, those who themselves hate it become vessels for misfortune, whereas those who take refuge in it [become vessels for prosperity].
By saying "they are possessed of fortune," the fact that they conform to anger and favor has been stated; and by this, the excellence of their divine endowment is all the more clearly indicated.

Immediately thereafter, he recalled his birth solely because of his firm resolve in giving a lump of sour gruel to the four ascetics. Through firm resolve, even unwholesome karma is exhausted by means of extreme spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). Therefore, in this case, there is a recollection of the self because of the nature of that desired formative action (*saṃskāra*).

For this very reason, it has been stated that even in another birth, there is a mere recollection and full comprehension of the power of giving within that very same uninterrupted birth; the implication is that otherwise, there would be an absence of the roots of merit that have been cultivated to such an extent. [This leads to] happiness of body and mind.
And its cause is the enjoyment of objects that have been easily obtained and the non-arising of suffering.

And its primary cause, its fundamental basis, is giving after having desisted from unwholesome deeds. He has thus described such giving as being more distinguished and endowed with supreme distinction.

Because the fruit of giving has been directly perceived. And regarding "the restraint of ethical discipline" (*śīlasaṃvara*), three kinds of ethical discipline have been taught: namely, abstention from misdeeds and the performance of truthful actions. Among these, *saṃvara* is the restraining or regulating of the influence of evils such as violence. As for the meaning of *śīla*:

He cultivated—that is, he nourished and protected—the state of having that become his very nature, which is appropriate for a householder; this is the meaning. And he observed the *poṣadha* vow, which is constant, excellent, and characterized by qualities such as being unbroken, not deficient, and not mottled; for it is called *poṣadha* because it bestows (*dadhati*) nourishment (*poṣam*) upon the side of wholesome qualities.
The restraint of the actions of mind, speech, and body is as it has been stated: from the killing of all living beings,
from taking what belongs to others, from unchaste conduct, likewise from divisive speech, from false speech, from intoxicants that produce negligence,
from [using] perfumes, garlands, dance, song, and amusements, and from high beds and seats.
"Today, having desisted, I shall practice the conduct of the Arhats through the eight qualities," and so forth.

On the festival days, such as the fifteenth day of the lunar month and others, since the word *poṣadha* itself signifies the sense of restraint (*niyama*), others explain that there is a distinct meaning from the word *niyama*. [1]

One whose heart-mind (*citta*) is "clear" (*pratīta*)—that is, manifest—is so described; the meaning is that his mind was joyful (*tuṣṭa-manas*).

Because there is certainty regarding the arising of the fruit of merit that is directly perceived. For this very reason, he will say "of certain meaning," which means that its meaning is non-deviant due to one's own experience. Regarding the phrase "the two verses":
because they are being recited, a *śloka* is also called a *gāthā*.

The Sugatas, the Buddhas, and the Samyaksambuddhas— these are the three types, including the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. For all of them, service and attendance performed with devotion through giving, honor, and so forth, according to one's ability, result in a very slight, even minimal, abundance of fruit— that is, a perfection of results.

The connection is with the phrase "of whose service. That [service] does not exist, because even the slightest service brings about great fruit and manifestation. And this has indeed been heard previously in former births; it is only due to the absence of direct experience that it is [now]... [that which is now].
"I speak from personal experience; see and understand this for yourself. To the question "What is that?", he says:

"The greatness of the abundance of the fruit"—the abundance (*vibhava*) of the fruit is its prosperity (*sampatti*), and its greatness is its extreme vastness. *Kulmāṣa* is boiled black gram (*māṣa-bhakta*); a ball made from that is a *piṇḍī*.
Because it has been kept overnight and is fit for consumption, it is dried out; for that very reason it is *aruṇā*, meaning somewhat red.
Because it is devoid of oiliness, it is rough (*rūkṣā*); by this, its inferiority is expressed.
By this, the collective *dvandva* (*samāhāradvandva*) is intended.

He makes known that even from such a lowly gift there arises the production of vast enjoyments;
"this is it" means that what was stated in general terms is now stated in detail.

"Chariots, horses," and so forth: this fourfold army of mine, this earth free from rivals, this sovereign splendor (*śrī*) which is full of affection and follows no other, these noble and excellent wives, and all this [wealth] resulting from the possession of every prosperity— [all this is yours].

"By the gift of such a lump of fermented gruel," he says; the meaning is: "Since this experience of mine has resulted from this, you all should be diligent in acts of giving. "Possessing the grace of intoxicated lordly elephants" refers to that army which has the specific, playful movements of great elephants; "not meager" means not small.
"Kevalā" means devoid of other kings. "Dhana" refers to the treasury; the meaning is that it is abundant and widely distributed.
The connection is as follows: "Behold the splendor—the excellence—of this collection, that is, the mass, of these fruits produced from lumps of boiled grain."

Those whose minds are not filled with curiosity do not venture—that is, they are unable—to question or to inquire further because of the King’s extreme profundity. "Niyatam" means you always speak necessarily. "Mudam" means joy or gladness at having spoken what was told. This...
The word "jana" points to the self and so forth that are present [in the context]. "Kim" is used in the sense of a question; "nu" expresses deliberation;
"iti" refers back to what was previously stated. I do not consider this to be a secret that ought not to be told, because a secret is never proclaimed in such a manner anywhere. And for this reason:

I too ask this openly and clearly. "In which outburst" (*udgare*) the purpose of the cause—the motive—is "unperceived," meaning not to be inferred; such is the case here. An "outburst" (*udgāra*) is the manifestation of a matter residing in the heart. The sense is that it is "agitated" due to curiosity, meaning it is restless.
The circle of ministers, whose minds were thus agitated, shaken, restless, and wavering by curiosity, was addressed by him with these words:
"Let it be heard by me— my inner apartments, the women of the harem, and the city, the people of the town."
The sense is: "Let it be understood; I shall tell you. In a dream—that is, during the state of sleep—[the phrase] *nāgendranīlam* [is used]. (Note: Ms reads *dānāś*; AJM(K) reads *'nāgendranilam*).

Just as one who has awakened clearly remembers what was experienced according to how it was experienced;

or, for example, just as one who has awakened from the state of sleep clearly recollects events that occurred on a previous day or similar occasion, so too did I exist, thinking, "I too [experienced] my own birth."

"I am one who has become [so]. The connection is as follows: for those who are exalted by wealth alone and not by conduct and so forth, there is a livelihood—a way of life—that is acquired from them, which is wretched and joyless.
"By action" means by the carrying of burdens and so forth; "propitiation" means the pleasing of lords through that [action].
Having acquired a livelihood through hardship.
Such as I am—of this very nature—[I am one for whom] maintenance is wages; that [maintenance] is like a hall, a dwelling place. Of what kind? He says: humiliation is contempt;
fatigue is the exhaustion of body, speech, and mind; wretchedness is the absence of joy. Desiring to enter into those [conditions]...

The connection [is as follows]: "Protection" means guarding against the fear of non-subsistence (*avṛtti*). It is with the intention and expectation that "here [in this place] you shall be my protector" that one desires to enter; having understood for oneself—rather than out of dependence on another—that the fear caused by non-subsistence will no longer exist, one wishes to enter.

"Desiring" means precisely this: [desiring] to go out from their homes for the sake of a livelihood. "Ascetics" (*śramaṇāḥ*) refers to those who exert themselves and practice austerity; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent according to the rule of the *bahulādhikāra*.
In this context, they should be understood as *pratyekabuddhas* and celibate practitioners (*brahmacāriṇas*), since at that time [there were no] perfectly awakened ones (*samyaksaṃbuddhas*).

Because of the absence of the appearance of a Buddha, there is also the absence of Śrāvakas. He saw four groups of four; he will say "in his own home," not in a monastery or similar place. The monks are those who have departed from the household life; their *lakṣmī* is their splendor.

With the activities of mind, speech, and body completely stilled, and with afflictions shaken off—that Fortune was made one with their very selves by them, such that it is perceived exactly as it is known; this is understood from the word *iva* (as if), meaning it was followed and pursued as if it were inherent to them. Through clarity, which is the departure of turbidity, it becomes gentle.

"Free from harshness; since such as you have come to my house," with a mind characterized by an excess of favor, I gave [the gift]. "Having prostrated"—that is, having bowed down intensely. And this intensity arises from bowing with body, speech, and mind. Thus, he is "restrained."

The meaning is that he is pure and respectful, because it is possible to act in such a manner at home; for that [purity] is the cause of that gift, just as the emergence of a sprout— the manifestation of a sprout— is the result of a seed.

Because it is obtained by our effort, it is "obtainable through effort" (*prayatnalabhya*); yet because it perishes without effort, it is "perishing without effort" (*ayatnanāśinī*). Since that worldly prosperity (*sampad*), which is the manifestation of power based on existence (*bhavāśrayā sāṃsārikī*), is [transient], therefore that [restraint] is satisfaction (*tṛpti*).

Even the pleasure of marks does not bring happiness; how much less will that lead to peace? For worldly prosperities, being pursued while based on existence, only generate craving. Alas, what else [could it be]? O human woman, give these beings—these very creatures—their due. Be intent upon them.
The meaning is: "those who are afflicted by the exhaustion and weariness resulting from that intense calamity and suffering which persists. My mind proceeds along the path of contentment;
therefore, the meaning is "by means of this merit. This word *rujā* has a meaning similar to *ruk*.
"By grace," meaning by the stainlessness of the mind, "the hairs of the body thrilled," that is to say, they stood on end.

This is "appropriate" and "fitting" for such an extraordinary resolve, which is otherwise unachievable. For this deed—such as the sacrifice of one's own body—has been undertaken with great determination.
"In that case, only great action is effective in accomplishing [the goal], not any other.

You ought to remember us; we entreat you with this in mind. Such is the request made because there is excessive zeal and intense devotion toward one's own welfare; otherwise, [one's concern] would be solely for the sake of all sentient beings.

What is to be sought from one who makes such an effort? For those like you, who do not perceive their own purpose as a task to be accomplished and remain ignorant, it is the self itself that is destroyed by causing such exertion; it is the self itself that is destroyed by the failure to produce happiness.
The self alone is thus accomplished. And that must be forgiven—that is, endured—by us. Our command is our teaching; it is a favor and a grace.
We shall fulfill its path and way according to one’s desire, with full confidence. That [path] we...
The meaning is "I shall show compassion. The word *khalu* is used as an ornament (*alaṃkāra*). This assistance is mine without effort;

for, having encountered one who seeks such [a goal] as this, I obtain the fruit of giving my own body. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no need to worry about being unable to endure [the task]. As for liberation...

Dharma. Like nectar because it destroys death, its distribution—namely, giving—I shall first perform for you alone. And for our mutual pleasure, the connection is that violence must be avoided, and greed for the property of others and the possessions of others must be abandoned.
By this, the speech of one who intends theft and the practice of falsehood have been mentioned. "Speech" (*vāk*) refers to discourse that is censurable;
the connection is that one should avoid that which is characterized by falsehood, harshness, slander, and idle chatter.
"Intoxicant" (*madya*) is that which causes intoxication, such as *surā* and the like; the delusion consisting of that evil is what is to be avoided. Thus it is connected.
Bondage.

Having been told "So be it" by the king, and having promised and accepted the five precepts for that king, they vanished on the spot; once vanished, at that very moment when the decision to give was made, the earth trembled in many ways. Thus he said.
Jātakamālāṭīkā, page 362.

In many ways, they have gone to Mount Sumeru, the mountain of gold; thus, "gone to Sumeru" (*sumerugatāḥ*). That flower, stirred by the wind, was like a cloud in the sky, in the atmosphere—so called because in some places it took the form of a mass (*paṭala*) resembling a lotus (*padma*)—like a flock (*senā*) of winged birds.

In some places—because they are horizontal; because they have a square shape like a canopy; having spread out and expanded like a garland because of their length; like a wreath, knotted and interwoven;
equally and simultaneously, pervading the entire sky on all sides, they were scattered and distributed.

Scattered. Because of that state of being—characterized by an intense, arisen, and agitated flurry (āvega) intended to turn back the lord of the earth, the king—the sound was greater than the natural [noise]. And by those waters whose sequence and movement [were thus affected]...
He whose body possessed vigor (*saujas*)—that is, existing splendor (*vidyamāna-tejas*)—on account of his marches, shone forth; he truly shone. This is the meaning:
it was understood that the great ocean, with its surging waters set in motion by an earthquake and accompanied by sound, was restraining the king.
"Having set out on his journey" (13)—this is because the ocean is by nature composed of water.
Perceiving that, the Lord of the Gods arrived with agitation—that is, with great respect—wondering, "What is this?
Having reflected upon and considered the cause of that disturbance of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), he [became] anxious...
"Having understood the interval" means having understood the situation. "The king Maitrībala’s misfortune" refers to his ruin;

there is the apprehension that it might occur through the depletion of his flesh and blood. "Therefore, quickly" (*tūrṇam*) and "speedily" (*tvaritam*) are adverbs modifying the action. "He went to the royal palace" means Śakra arrived at the king's residence.

"Out of grief caused by the king's oppression and fear that we are now to be devoured by yakṣas, he was extremely agitated— that is, exceedingly distressed. Furthermore, even though the king had fallen into such a state, seeing the serenity of his countenance, he was filled with extraordinary wonder.

Śakra, having approached and presented himself before that king, praised— that is, extolled— his deed with a charming and captivating voice, [bestowing] grace, which is the clarity of the mind. 11 Ms reads *samaye va*.

[He spoke of] its greatness: "The earth, tender through its favor toward others and skillful, has indeed become exceedingly well-protected—possessing a protector through being offered to you, and having you as its master through being accepted by you.
Having thus praised and lauded him, [he spoke of] the immediate healing of wounds, the immediate growth of sores.

In that regard, he is capable. *Nirvedana* means free from affliction (*apagatavyatha*). *Pratipūjita* refers to Śakra. *Bahukara* means those who perform much assistance. By the words "fearing the day" (*divāvibheti*) and so forth, there is the suffix *-tap*.
It may be thought: "having intended this. The meaning is: "having kept this very thing in mind. "These" (*ete*).
"O monks, there are five. || ||

Valor is heroism. Policy is the fivefold counsel. Discipline consists of modesty and lack of arrogance, since mastery over the senses has already been mentioned. This [lineage] has been attained through family tradition.
The prosperity (*śrī*) or power (*vibhūti*) that results from the complete subjugation and defeat of the enemy is such [prosperity].

"Vṛddhas" refers to those possessed of knowledge; the rule of attending upon them is the non-transgression of their instructions, and for that reason. The three Vedas—the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman*—are the *Trayi*. *Anvīkṣikī*...
One who has perceived the true nature of these two through the science of reasoning (*tarkavidyā*) is one who knows them as such.
By "constituents" (*prakṛtibhiḥ*) is meant the seven constituents— sovereign, minister, realm, fort, treasury, army, and ally— the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) shines when manifested by them.
He who possesses that is "he who has such [a state]. Here, *daṇḍa* means governance;
its *nīti* is the leading forth, which is correct application. Because of its being free from blemish and because of the absence of weariness, there is no distress.
*Vārttā* consists of agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade. Its *vidhi* is the rule, the arrangement, and the performance thereof.

"Artha" refers to one whose purpose is correctly engaged; by this, proficiency in the four branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) is indicated. There was a kingdom named Śibi, and he became its sovereign king.
Furthermore, this king is described as being righteous (*dharma*), because the Bodhisattva was present here.

That very [example] will serve as an illustration; it is appropriate to describe him by means of the qualities of a bodhisattva. Even his taking up of the religious life (*upādāna*) is solely for the purpose of proclaiming the qualities of this bodhisattva; otherwise, how could one who has gone forth into such hardship abandon wife, children, and so forth in the forest?

If even the father were devoid of virtues, he would nonetheless cause [the son] to go forth in such a manner; therefore, he describes him as well with the words beginning "by the arising of virtues. Just as a cave protected by lions—that is, guarded by lions—is unassailable by wild beasts, so too is this [place].
Thus his royal splendor is desirable. Now, [let us consider] his knowledge of the specific qualities [of the Vedas]:
the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and Atharva.

9. [The author] shows that they are seekers of deer and possessors of knowledge through the passage beginning with "in asceticism" (*tapaḥsu*). Those who have exerted themselves in asceticism and the like are ascetics; those who know the sciences are experts in the arts. These [qualities] are present in him whose assembly (*sadaḥ*) or court (*sabhā*) they have entered.

"Great honor" (*bahumāna*) refers to a specific degree of respect. Others say that "endowed with that" means they went (*īyuḥ*) with a particular [degree of] giving, honor, and so forth. And those whose greatness was being manifested by those very royal honors (*rājakiyapūjā*)—that is, by the king's reception (*pratipatti*)—[were such].

"Without interval" means uninterrupted. "Renowned" means manifest; the meaning is that he is filled with those multitudes of virtues. This very Blessed One is Śākyamuni. "Free from arrogance" means devoid of pride. Those whose fame has a visible extent—
The word "fear" (*bhī*) is connected [to the preceding]; and because it functions as a qualifier (*gamaka*), there is a compound, meaning "while those directions exist.

Heaven, earth, and the netherworld constitute the triad of worlds (*lokatraya*). For others, there was not only no enthusiasm to spread even fragments of their fame—mere vestiges of glory—but not even the space [to do so].

There was not even a place [for them]; this is *tulyayogitā*. Those arisings of suffering (*duḥkhodaya*) pertaining to the world—that is, pertaining to *saṃsāra*, such as disease, separation, and so forth—the arrogance (*avalepa*), the pride (*darpa*), which consists in the overcoming of all the world through their abundance or power; [he], being unable to endure it, that is, unable to tolerate it...

He entered into, that is, he engaged in, a battle-struggle against the arising of suffering, a conflict involving intense combat. How so? It is said: he whose nature it was to rain down *dāna*s as arrows, and who possessed a great bow made of compassion itself.

Likewise, out of compassion for the practice of giving, through the distribution of wealth— that is, the bestowing of riches— he would mount his excellent elephant on festival days such as the full moon and inspect the *sattrāgāras*, the halls of charity.
"He looked at him" is the connection [of the sentence]. "Resembling a peak of the Snowy Mountain" means white and large. "His face adorned with streaks of rut."¹¹ ¹¹ Ms:

The meaning is "only" (*mātra*). The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of elephants are those indicating good or bad fortune; [this refers to] their training (*vinaya*).

The undertaking of the training [1], speed, impetus, strength, and the majesty of gods, nāgas, and so forth—being endowed with these, he is "excellent. For excellence is not said to exist by mere presence alone. Thus, the meaning is this: he is auspicious by virtue of his marks; he is supreme by virtue of discipline, speed, and strength.
He whose scent of rut, when smelled, causes other elephants to break [in submission] is a *gandhahastin*.

He is "well-known" (*samājñāta*), renowned among all kings. "To be ridden by them" means suitable for a royal vehicle (*rājavāhana*); "to be trained, harnessed, and ridden" refers to the three categories of work (*karmaskandha*), of which the third is the best.

(12) "The mass of karma" means [it is] like this: situated on all sides around the city, they stand as watering places for those who seek their needs, just as ponds and the like exist in the forest for the drinking of deer and birds.

[It is] the place where those seeking [gifts] are known to arrive; because of satisfying them, [it is] their own [or] belonging to themselves. Whether or not they are of use to those who come as supplicants—this is the investigation, that is, the examination; and "in that same way" means by that very manner for a person who delights in giving.

And this is a general statement regarding him: "the one immediately following the earth" means the sovereign of the mandala immediately following. He can be deceived or outwitted. His passion for giving is under the power of pure capacity; he is subject to that. There, in the capital city of Saṃjaya—

"I made a vow; I have made it," is the meaning, which is to say, "I established it. Those whose right hands were raised up, lifted, and extended—those with their right hands thus positioned—stood together in front, that is, in the presence of the city-king.

The *ātmanepada* ending is used here according to the rule *samavapravibhyaḥ sthalam*. "Having restrained" (*vinigṛhya*) means having first controlled the elephant and established it in a motionless state. "He questioned them"—that is, he asked the Brahmins—"let it be commanded; let an order be given."
He cannot even endure the begging of supplicants; having given them his command, the meaning is "take [what you need].

"Gativilāsa" means the grace of movement; by that, he is "vilambi," moving slowly. By means of his qualities—such as *lakṣaṇa* (auspicious marks) and *vinaya* (discipline)—which serve as the instruments, those [qualities] of yours arise from your generosity and heroism.
"And we have come because of our desire for this cause"—this is the connection.
"Cirasya" is an indeclinable (nipāta) resembling a word ending in the genitive case; it means "after a long time.
"Upon the noble request," that is, upon the petition for the royal elephant, "sumukhaṃ" means with a cheerful face, clearly [indicating satisfaction].
"Indeed"; the word "indeed" (*tu*) is used for emphasis, meaning "quite clearly. Regarding the "application of wretchedness":

having been entreated by these Brahmins, [the elephant] must be taken [by force]. Wretchedness (*dīnatva*) consists in the loss of hope and the absence of joy. By employing these Brahmins, he has asked for the elephant; this is his infamy (*ayaśas*).

And by this deception and fraud, that which is unrighteous (*adharma*)— namely, disregarding and setting aside both fame and righteousness (*yaśodharma*), and appearing as if intent upon our welfare while actually contemplating our harm through the seizing of the elephant— he has indeed commenced what is beneficial for us, since the arrival of supplicants occurs through such a gift.

The connection is as follows: although he was learned and even knew the science of kingship (*rājaśāstra*), which consists of the path and method of dharma arrived at through the pursuit and practice of worldly interests; that is, the science of kingship wherein the acquisition of dharma occurs without conflict with worldly interests.

The meaning is as follows: If he knew [the consequences], why did he give? He says: "Out of devotion to *dharma*, he gave without regard for the treatises on worldly profit (*artha-śāstra*). (11) He was not shaken—that is, not moved—by the deceit of policy or by the faults inherent in such policy, because of his devotion to *dharma* and his great-souled nature. Gold...

He was one whose beautiful ornaments, such as the *nakṣatramālā* and others, were made of networks of clusters of gold. The word "city" (*nagara*) refers here to the citizens by metonymy (*tātsthya*). It was thoroughly agitated—that is, shaken—due to their partiality toward [the prince's] policy; thus, this [prince] has been rendered unrighteous (*anaya*) by the crown prince.
Thus [it was] by means of awakening.
The *Jātakamālātīkā*:
that tumultuous clamor which, through its formalities and allurements, constitutes a constraint, has been loosened in his speech and action. "O King" is the address. Thus [he was] deceived...

The sense is that he was being praised by the crown prince. To endure—that is, to forgive—the calamity or affliction of his own kingdom; [the elephant] whose face is its trunk, which is attended by bees intoxicated by the drinking of rut, and which, having partaken of the ichor (madas), is fragrant with it.
The wind [dispels] the arrogance of rut and the pride of intoxication belonging to rival elephants;
it removes them. "Exertion" refers to that caused by battle and the like. "Suffering therein" refers to that caused by blows and so forth.
Without those, merely by smelling his scent alone, the rival elephants [are overcome] by his rut.
The meaning is that they become such. By whose splendor—that is, by your splendor—[they] are overcome and eclipsed.

Those whose power is the influence of the fourfold army (caturaṅgabala) are so described. They, your enemies, are conquered; this victory is embodied, possessing form; it is taken away, led to another land, [to] a foreign kingdom.
"O King"—this is an address. "Worthy of being given" (*deyarūpam*) means suitable for a gift; *rūpa* is used here in the sense of praise.

"Fixed" (*niyatā*) means certain. Thus, how will the royal fortune (*rājalakṣmī*) seek out this Viśvaṃtara, who is proceeding by this very path of policy (*nayavimārgeṇa*), which is born of right conduct?
"He will follow correctly" means "not at all. "Purā agrataḥ" means "at another time. He gladdens, and will gladden, your enemies (*vidviṣaḥ* = *śatrūn*).
[The rule applies to] the particles *yāvat* and *purā* when followed by a verb form.

Taking Śibi and others as examples, he was indeed displeased; yet, out of regard for what must be done, he acted like Viśvantara, appearing agitated and as if angry. Having said, "It is exactly as you say," and having thus accepted [the challenge], [he gave away] that which was like vomit—[the flesh] vomited from his own body.
"Who will bring it back? Who will take it back?"—the intention is: "No one has been given; let this [child] be led away. "A measure"—that is, he will establish a small restriction.

Regarding faults such as women, gambling, and liquor, he who turns away from engagement in them and [turns toward] virtues— 1. *vimukhasya*: "of one who is turned away" (genitive singular masculine). The text fragment provided ends with this term. The following portion (*yasya guṇeṣu*) appears to be the beginning of a subsequent clause describing that person. The translation reflects the available text.
The meaning is that those who lack fortitude create attachments and indulgences regarding renunciation and other virtues.

Would the binding or the slaying of that son of one’s own body—that is, one born of the breast—be an adequate ransom or compensation for the elephant that was given? Is it for this reason that you speak thus?
Viśvantara cannot be dealt with in this matter by mere reproach;
rather, he must be killed or imprisoned because of this excessive addiction to giving.
Those whose fury, distress, or anger has been aroused and manifested are thus described. He approves [of this].

He wishes to have [this] made. We say that because he is righteous by nature, gentle out of compassion, and capable of enduring the unbearable agitation of the burden of kingship. Those by whom the word "splendor" (*tejas*) has been attained are thus described; the meaning is "the majestic ones. Likewise, the threefold aim (*trivarga*)—dharma...

Those who are skilled (*nipuṇāḥ*) and proficient (*kuśalāḥ*) in serving and honoring him for the sake of their welfare and desires occupy his lion-throne; the meaning is that they exercise sovereignty. One from whom indifference has departed regarding policy is "one free from negligence in policy" (*nayanirapekṣaḥ*). Such a person, being righteous in nature (*dharmātmakaḥ*), [resides] in the forest of asceticism (*tapovana*).
This Viśvantara is not fit for the seat of honor; that is to say, he is not fit to occupy the lion-throne.

Those faults resulting from misconduct committed by kings who are lords of the earth ripen upon their dependent servants according to their will; yet, even so, such [consequences] are seen among these very servants.

Even those things that cause harm to oneself must indeed be endured; however, they are not to be endured by kings—this is the connection [of the sentence]. Why? He says: "Because of the obstruction of the root," meaning because it causes the destruction of the kingdom.
